## Overview

The **ATLAS detector** is a large particle detector at CERN's Large Hadron Collider.
Protons or heavy ions collide near its center, producing particles that travel
through several specialized layers. Each layer supplies a different piece of
information, helping scientists reconstruct what happened in a collision.

ATLAS is approximately 46 metres long and 25 metres in diameter. The illustration
below shows a cutaway of this enormous instrument, revealing systems that would
normally be hidden inside its outer structure.

## How the Detector Works

The innermost tracking system records the paths of charged particles. A magnetic
field bends those trajectories, allowing their momenta to be reconstructed.
Calorimeters measure the energy deposited by electrons, photons, and hadrons.
Farther out, muon chambers record muons that pass through the inner systems.
Together, these measurements help reconstruct the particles produced in a collision.

## Calorimetry

ATLAS calorimeters measure particle energy by sampling the showers produced as
particles pass through alternating **absorber** and **active** layers. The system
combines a central steel-and-scintillator Tile calorimeter with liquid-argon (LAr)
calorimeters covering the electromagnetic, hadronic end-cap, and forward regions.

Select **Full Detector** to view the official labelled calorimeter cutaway, or choose
**R–z Layout** to examine the longitudinal arrangement near the beam axis.

::: {.column-body}

```{=html}
{{< include /detectors/components/atlas-calorimetry.html >}}
```

:::

**Electromagnetic calorimeters (EMB and EMEC).** The LAr electromagnetic barrel
(EMB) and electromagnetic end-cap (EMEC) measure showers initiated primarily by
electrons and photons. Layers of lead absorbers and liquid argon provide fine spatial
sampling of deposited energy.

**Tile hadronic calorimeters.** A central barrel and two extended barrels use steel
absorbers and scintillating tiles to sample hadronic showers. These measure much
of the energy carried by strongly interacting particles in the central region.

**Hadronic end-cap calorimeters (HEC).** Located at larger angles to the beam than
the FCal, the HEC uses copper absorbers and liquid argon to measure hadronic energy
in the end-cap region.

**Forward calorimeters (FCal).** Close to the beam axis, the FCal extends coverage
to approximately $3.1 < |\eta| < 4.9$. Each end-cap contains three LAr modules:
**FCal1** uses copper absorbers for electromagnetic showers, while **FCal2** and
**FCal3** use tungsten absorbers for hadronic showers. In the R–z view, their order
along the beam direction is visible alongside the EMEC and HEC modules.

## Follow a Particle

Different particles leave different signatures. For example, an electron
usually deposits much of its energy in the electromagnetic calorimeter, while
a muon can travel through the calorimeters and reach the outer muon chambers.

## What Parts of the Detector I Use in My Analysis

My heavy-ion analyses mainly combine two detector measurements: **charged-particle
tracks in the Inner Detector** and **forward transverse energy in the FCal**.
They probe different regions of a collision and serve distinct purposes.

### Inner Detector: Charged-Particle Tracking

The Inner Detector is the main ATLAS system for reconstructing charged particles
near midrapidity. It surrounds the beam pipe with several nested tracking layers,
so particles emerging from the collision leave a sequence of spatial measurements
as they move outward through the detector.

::: {.column-body}

```{=html}
{{< include /detectors/components/atlas-tracking.html >}}
```

:::

In broad terms, tracking works in three steps. First, the **Pixel detector**, the
**silicon microstrip tracker (SCT)**, and the **transition radiation tracker (TRT)**
record discrete position measurements, usually called **hits**. Second, pattern-
recognition algorithms identify groups of hits that belong to the same particle and
fit them to a common trajectory. Third, because the particle moves in the ATLAS
solenoidal magnetic field, the trajectory bends: the amount of curvature determines
the transverse momentum $p_{\mathrm{T}}$, while the direction of curvature identifies
the sign of the electric charge. The fitted trajectory also gives the particle's
direction and point of closest approach to the collision vertex.

For my analyses, these reconstructed tracks provide the charged particles whose
event-by-event kinematics are used to study multiplicity, mean transverse momentum,
and collective behavior in heavy-ion collisions. The tracking system is therefore
the detector element that directly measures the particles entering the core physics
observables.

### Forward Calorimeters: Event Selection and Centrality

The forward calorimeters measure transverse energy at large pseudorapidity,
separated from the midrapidity tracks used in my analysis. Their summed energy
provides an estimator of **collision centrality**, which is closely related to the
overlap geometry of the colliding nuclei.

Using forward energy for event classification and inner-detector tracks for the
physics observables helps reduce **self-correlations**: if the same particles were
used both to select an event class and to calculate the observable, the selection
could introduce artificial correlations. The separation between tracking and
forward calorimetry is therefore an important part of the analysis strategy.
